sections.h2: What makes selling a house in Xenia, Ohio different?
sections.html:
Xenia is the Greene County seat, about 15 miles east of Dayton in the Miami Valley, and its housing history is shaped by storms. A tornado rated F5 crossed the middle of the city on April 3, 1974, during the Super Outbreak. It killed 34 people, injured 1,150, destroyed almost half of the city's buildings and left 10,000 people homeless. Another tornado hit on September 20, 2000, and was rated F4.

The city's own history menu still carries a page titled "Xenia Lives!" about the 1974 recovery, and the city keeps a system of tornado sirens. A seller who can hand a buyer receipts for a recent roof, siding or storm repair has useful paperwork, because storm history is an obvious question in Xenia.

The Census Bureau estimates 26,425 residents as of July 1, 2025, up 3.8% from the April 2020 estimates base of 25,447. That is the fastest growth of the four cities QuickFacts compares here.

sections.h2: What do Census numbers say about Xenia homes and owners?
sections.html:
The Xenia numbers sit between a college-town market and a heavily rental city. Census QuickFacts for 2020 to 2024 gives the figures below.

  • Owner-occupied rate: 60.9%, with a median owner-occupied value of $162,400.
  • Median gross rent: $931, the highest of the four Ohio cities QuickFacts lists beside Xenia (Wooster, Youngstown and Zanesville).
  • 10,765 households averaging 2.32 people.
  • 22.4% of residents are under 18, and 20.4% are 65 or older.
  • Mean travel time to work is 24.6 minutes, the longest of the four. The city's website carries a page for people relocating to Wright-Patterson Air Force Base.
  • Median household income is $56,029, and 17.9% of residents are in poverty.

Wikipedia describes Xenia as centrally placed in a transportation triangle formed by I-70, I-71 and I-75, reached by U.S. 35, U.S. 42 and U.S. 68. A listing can state the highway access plainly, since buyers who drive to Dayton or beyond will check it.

sections.h2: Which Xenia schools and neighborhoods do buyers ask about?
sections.html:
Xenia Community Schools serves the city with a preschool, five elementary schools (Cox, McKinley, Arrowood, Shawnee and Tecumseh), Warner Middle School and Xenia High School. Private options include Legacy Christian Academy and St. Brigid School. The Greene County Public Library has its main branch and administrative offices in the city.

Several city landmarks come up in showings. The Little Miami Scenic Trail runs through Xenia Station, and the city carries the nickname "Bicycle Capital of the Midwest," and five of its six former rail roadbeds have been converted to trail use. The Greene County Fairgrounds hosts the annual Dayton Hamvention, which Wikipedia says typically draws more than 20,000 amateur radio enthusiasts. If your house sits near the fairgrounds, mention the event traffic in your showing notes so buyers are not surprised.

sections.h2: How do Xenia zoning and property maintenance rules affect a sale?
sections.html:
The city's Planning and Zoning Division handles zoning permits and also oversees enforcement of the property maintenance code, which sets minimum standards for safe and sanitary buildings. It is in the City Administration Building at 107 East Main Street, open Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., and its phone number is 937-372-6389.

Two practical points for sellers:

  • The city's project list includes a "Zoning Update 2026." Ask Planning and Zoning whether the update changes the rules for your lot, an addition or an accessory building before you promise a buyer a particular use.
  • Code enforcement is a separate page on the city site from the Building Division. If you have received a notice about grass, debris or a structure, resolve it with that office before you list so the buyer's title and inspection reports come back clean.

The Planning and Zoning page sits under the city's Development Services Department, which is the place to start with a question about an unpermitted porch, deck or garage.

sections.h2: How does Greene County value a Xenia house, and when can you appeal?
sections.html:
The Greene County Auditor values property by mass appraisal, building a table from sales data in each area and testing it against actual sales. The auditor's FAQ notes that Ohio does not allow foreclosure sales in that analysis because they are not arm's-length sales, so a distressed sale next door should not drag your value down in the county's model.

A triennial update happens every three years without a visual inspection, and a full revaluation with a physical review happens in the sixth year. If you believe the appraised value is too high, you can file a complaint with the Greene County Board of Revision between January 1 and March 31. The auditor's FAQ also says there is no dollar-for-dollar link between a change in value and a change in taxes, because the voted levies are applied to the value.

Homestead rules and income limits change over time, so ask the Greene County Auditor for the current application and limits rather than relying on an old figure.

sections.h2: What happens to property taxes if a Xenia house is damaged by a tornado or fire?
sections.html:
Ohio gives the county board of revision a specific tool. Under Ohio Revised Code 323.17, when taxable real property has been destroyed or damaged by fire, flood, tornado or otherwise by at least 25% of its listed value, and at least $2,000 of taxable value, the board may by resolution extend the time to pay taxes on that property for up to one year past the normal due date.

The resolution is filed with the county auditor and treasurer and names the owner, the parcel and the board's estimate of the damage. If you are selling a storm-damaged house, ask the Greene County Auditor how to request the extension, and tell the title company about it so the closing statement shows what is still owed.

sections.h2: Who handles the deed, recording and transfer fee in a Xenia sale?
sections.html:
Three offices touch the deed. The signature must be acknowledged before a notary, judge, clerk of court, county auditor, county engineer or mayor (Ohio Revised Code 5301.01). The auditor endorses the conveyance after the buyer files a statement of value, and the grantor pays the conveyance fee and any county transfer tax (Ohio Revised Code 319.202). The deed is then recorded with the county recorder, and an unrecorded deed can lose out to a later buyer who had no notice of it (Ohio Revised Code 5301.25).

sections.h2: When does a cash offer make sense for a Xenia house?
sections.html:
A cash offer fits when a house needs work that a mortgage appraisal would flag, such as an older roof, a damp basement or deferred maintenance. It also fits an inherited house or a rental where the owner lives out of town.

Ask each buyer for a written offer, who pays closing costs, and the closing date. Compare those against the net you would receive after agent commission and repairs on a regular listing. Ask the title company for the settlement statement before the signing date so every line makes sense.

faqs.q: Does Xenia require a disclosure form when I sell?
faqs.a: Yes, for a house of one to four units. Ohio Revised Code 5302.30 requires the seller to give each prospective buyer a signed state disclosure form as soon as practicable. Exceptions include transfers by an estate fiduciary, to a spouse or lineal relative, and to a buyer who has lived in the home for a year.

faqs.q: Does Greene County count a foreclosure sale when it sets values?
faqs.a: No. The auditor's FAQ says Ohio does not allow foreclosure sales in the county's analysis because they are not arm's-length sales. Ordinary sales in your area are what the appraisal tables are tested against.

faqs.q: Is my Xenia house covered by a tax extension if a tornado damaged it?
faqs.a: Possibly. Ohio Revised Code 323.17 lets the county board of revision extend the payment date for up to one year when damage is at least 25% of the listed value and at least $2,000 of taxable value. Contact the Greene County Auditor for the process.

faqs.q: Where do I ask about zoning for a house in Xenia?
faqs.a: Call the city's Planning and Zoning Division at 937-372-6389 or visit 107 East Main Street between 8:00 a.m. and 4:00 p.m. on weekdays. Ask about the Zoning Update 2026 project if you plan to sell with an addition or a second structure.

faqs.q: How long can I wait to appeal my Greene County value?
faqs.a: Complaints are accepted each year from January 1 through March 31. The filing is for the value that sets your tax bill, and it does not change the voted levy rates.
